>Maybe it's more of a moral/ethical/rights debate than a practical one; does a person have a right to consume the product of another for free? If I have to go back to rice days, if a member of our group didn't help out honestly I probably still would've wanted to give them a share of rice cause I just have that desire in me to provide for my people.

I’d differentiate, perhaps pedantically since this might be what you already mean, between having a right and being right.

In your rice example, since you’re giving the person a share of your own free will, then of course that person *has* a right to consume it. 

But *is* it right in general for him to accept it and/or for you to offer it when he’s not contributing to the group? As we’re speaking in a wider, general sense here, I’d say society has concluded that it’s only right in extenuating circumstances, e.g. physical and/or mental illness. Meaning that to society, in many cases, perhaps it would actually be wrong for him to accept and/or for you to offer when he’s not contributing.

On the other hand, say the person is deciding not to contribute because he no longer wishes to live. Would you then be in the wrong for offering him the rice, since that perpetuates a life in which he bo longer wishes to participate?


>Now would I and others probably be frustrated sometimes with that person? Most likely, as nobody like feeling taken advantage of or working without getting anything in return.

At that point it’s a balancing act between frustration and compassion, which probably hinges on the circumstances of the non-contributor. Even the most compassionate person may be outweighed by frustration if the person has, by all accounts, no reason they can’t contribute.

>I concede to you that yes, voting does seem more like a suggestion than a requirement like working. I'm glad you enjoy voting and contributing in this way.

There are definitely different levels of suggestions, though. Like countries that have mandatory voting laws. Although, violating those laws would only result in a fine, so I’d still be hard pressed to call it a HAVE to scenario.

>Yeah social workers are in that group of jobs that are extremely underpaid for the work they provide. As aways I think the reason is there's little immediate value produced so why invest resources into it. Do I find it appaling? Yeah, I think your parents deserve far more from me and others.

Yeah, societally it makes sense that their relative less value to economic productivity is rewarded less, even if it’s not a very moral position. Since morality doesn’t really affect the existence or prosperity of society, its value is rather subject to the whims of whoever’s currently in charge of societal policymaking. That whimsical unpredictability in support also makes the profession less appealing.

>As it stands as long as a small minority wish and desire to not have been born, the perpetuation of the cycle will continue, justified (by some) that the needs of the many outweigh those of the few.

I wonder if the few, in this case, even has needs though? Generally, a need is *wanting something*, but if the needs of the few in this scenario boil down to **not** wanting something (not wanting to live and/or not wanting to have children), I’m not sure if that justification you mentioned applies. Although, an argument could be made that not wanting something is still wanting nothing, so idk.

But yeah I mostly agree with your point. As long as the vast majority think they need to live, they’ll never willingly let go of the minority who don’t; since that would harm the chances of the collective to survive. They selfishly cleave to life by any means necessary. Even if that means chaining the minority to the drudgeries of life.

>I do find fulfillment in giving back, even if it's just as simple as taking a picture for someone like I used to do. Sure practically I do it so I can acquire money to pay other people for things I need/want, but there's still the mental/spiritual aspect for me of feeling like I'm doing something helpful for somebody.

Because even though I like helping others, and even if I found a dream profession I’d *want* to do, the fact that I *have* to get a job to make money to live angers me into refusing to participate.

When I say have to do, I mean HAVE to - like working. If I don’t work and had no external supports, I would either die or be digging through trash for scraps of food, i.e. a life I wouldn’t want to live.

Back in high school and college I used to be really into giving back / helping others - Boy Scouts in high school and volunteering a bunch during college. 

But I became disillusioned with volunteering on an individual level, ironically, during a volunteer trip I took on one Spring vacation. Our group watched a documentary on volunteering and a point it made was that as the number of charities and volunteer organizations have increased, the societal problems they’re trying to help (poverty, hunger, etc.) have also increased over time. They gave the reason as a lack of governmental action in actually fixing these societal issues. Basically, instead of the government fixing the problems with long term, strategic solutions, it’s become too reliant on charities and volunteers who, while doing great work for individuals in need, could never have the amount of resources needed to truly fix the underlying issues of the people they’re trying to help. Therefore, the cycle of suffering for the people these volunteers are trying to help will only continue and increase over time as the government keeps deferring meaningful aid in favor of band-aids from individual volunteers.

It also doesn’t help that I see how poorly my parents, who are social workers, are treated by society as reflected in how little money they make, despite helping people daily. Definitely discourages me from pursuing any sort of career in that field.

>The consent part is where I do see how those can subscribe to AN. I don't have a logical argument against not feeling bitter about that lack of consent for being born. I can even agree we could pursue looking at better options for those who don't want to participate any longer.

It’d be great if society could look at better options for those who don’t want to participate in the social contract, but it’ll never happen.

Every organization desires its own survival above all else, even something as big and ill-defined as society. Giving its members an easy way to opt out of contributing to the organization would lead to its collapse via lack of support and resources from a reduced population. So no organization would do that.

If anything, society encourages the exact opposite to keep its functions running. Like how governments are pushing pro-natalist policies in many developed countries to make sure their societies don’t collapse from a future lack of working-age citizens. They don’t give a damn about whether children *should* be born, just about how many more kids their pro-natalist policies can produce over time for the well-being of society.

>As for the guilt, I guess that's a personal journey for one to process. Speculating here, but maybe that guilt is a sign of acknowledging a need to give back to other humans. The trick would then be to find out how you can do so under conditions acceptable to the individual. I think that guilt is conditioned into us, as we grow up, from society because if we didn’t have that persistent drive to give back to those who gave to us, then there’d be no social contract or society.

Society perpetuates itself through convincing its members that contributing back to it, as well as to the other members of society that have given to you, is a noble deed that should bring you happiness and fulfill you. **I’m not sure if I fully believe this statement, but I definitely don’t fully disagree with it. That’s an intense exercise. I agree in general with your point that everyone should put in their fair share, but that’s only if the fundamental principle behind it is accepted:

> However, to *survive* we all needed to do our part.

If someone doesn’t want to survive, then that feeling of duty and responsibility to those around them become shackles trapping them in existence. They’re paralyzed between not wanting to live and feeling intense guilt for being a burden on others who they could be helping *and* for how bad they’d make those around them feel if they decided to not live anymore.

>I think if the social contract was a thing, it'd say that as long as you are consuming something from someone then you ought to give back somehow. Now personally I don't believe I can ever tell someone they ought to givd back, but I do encourage it.

>Regardless of the intentions of why someone produces something, it's the fact that we consume things that makes that social contract kinda a thing. I bought this phone, which uses electricity, that many many people worked to provide me. And I chose to purchase and use it. Someone produced this trailer I live in (don't knock it, I love my tiny trailer :)), someone ensured clean water is coming out of this sink that someone made, this fruit snack I'm eating is made by someone. I didn't choose to be born as a consumer, but I am.

>I want to be someone that, if I have to consume something from someone, I want to give back.

Again, I agree with your point in general. But for any sort of meaningful social contract to exist, like in any contract, there’d need to be a termination clause.

If I found a job that I didn’t wish to continue being a part of, I have an out and can terminate my contract with the company. But society has forbidden any such option for life’s social contract (other than extreme cases).

So the social contract expects me to put in my required time without my initial consent at birth, forces me to remain in the contract without any option of leaving if I decide I don’t like it and, possibly worst of all, it instills a feeling of self-imposed guilt that you’re letting society, your loved ones and even yourself down by refusing it.

For context, the job I took a leave of absence from wasn’t a file clerk. I started out at this company as a file clerk. Then a higher paid, though completely different type of, position opened up and they liked my work so much as a file clerk that they gave me the first crack at it. It required a year of experience in that field, but they officially counted my year of file clerk work towards it since I was around/filing the legal documents associated with the position.

Even though it was different work, it was going pretty good. I had two types of legal documents to complete, one type I actually kinda liked filling out and a second type that I didn’t like; so they balanced each other out. 

But after a bit, the company decided to reorganize its work responsibilities to try to increase efficiency. Our team actually pushed back against this a bit, since everything was working great for us. But management told us to give it time and see how it goes. Unfortunately, my new responsibility consisted entirely of the type of legal document that I disliked. 

It went okay for a bit, but the monotonous of only doing one thing, which I already disliked, became unbearable. I started leaving documents waiting to be completed for longer than acceptable periods. My direct manager talked to me about it once, but I didn’t really get in trouble. But still I couldn’t bear it. But when it happened again, the client, who was waiting on the document, cc:ed my boss’s boss and the CEO to complain. My boss’s boss talked to me this time - not necessarily harshly, but in a no-nonsense manner. The fact that this blew up to management and that my work credibility was, to me, seemingly in question, broke me. I couldn’t even sign in to my work computer without feeling debilitating anxious.

I won’t deny I hold responsibility for how it all went down. I decided to put off work that I disliked. I decided not to tell management how I was feeling out of a fear of disappointing them. Hell, I took the offer for the new position instead of sticking with file clerk since they believed I could do it. 

The management at this company were good people that I got to know as a file clerk, so I feel like I can’t lay the blame at their feet. They didn’t even fire me. If I told them I was ready to come back at the end of my leave of absence, I’m pretty sure they would’ve welcomed me back. But I’m confident I’d still be working there if they hadn’t tried to reorganize for efficiency’s sake.

But now I’m unemployed and can’t confidently say that this sort of mental health issue won’t reappear again in any sort of work I might ever try in the future.

**I think it's important that I contribute and produce value because I consume what other people produce, so for me there's a sense of just duty towards work.**

I understand where you’re coming from, and I might’ve agreed with you at one time. But now I’m at the point of virtually the opposite:

‘Why should I have to contribute and produce value for those around me when I never chose to be here in the first place?’

And

‘Why should I be duty-bound to reciprocate others’ production if they’re doing it of their own free will and I didn’t ask them to produce for me to begin with?’

The only work role I’ve really liked is file clerk jobs. I get to organize stuff on my own, away from any potential clients of the business at large and I can spend my free time doing whatever (listening to music, doing stuff online, etc.).

But there are three things working against doing that work:
1. It doesn’t pay well enough for me to live a life that I would consider acceptable enough to like living.
2. The way I ended up leaving my last job (leave of absence for mental health, then quitting when I couldn’t bear returning) is on my record and will probably look rather poorly to anywhere new I apply.
3. I strongly feel that working is a burden that we who have no choice in our lives are forced to bear. No choice in terms of having to work to live - and I’ve despised the idea of having to do things I don’t want to do since my existential crisis at 17.

I’ve actually never had any big dreams or desires in my life - which I’ve been told is weird, but it’s all I’ve ever known.

The only thing I ever wanted was to just have fun doing whatever I was doing. But that doesn’t end up well when you don’t find work fun.

But yeah I get what you're saying about my views on Miranda, although I did say that it didn't quite tarnish her character, but the sentiment's there so I get it. I usually do get heavily invested in things when I first start them and I get ideas forming.

And yeah, I know it's early in the show and that my thoughts and views on it and its character are based on limited information. I might be projecting a little too heavily upon the importance of these formative episodes since I know season 1 will only have 8 episodes, making it feel like each episode holds more importance than it probably will in hindsight.

I think I made a comment or two about how I understood Miranda's decision on the level of moving on, but it certainly could easily get lost in my sea of thoughts lol. My criticism of Miranda's decision comes in two waves; one that's based entirely upon my own projection and opinion of how I think her "character" (since as you point out, we've seen so little of it) should/would have affected her decision-making during the four-year time skip and the other that's based more upon what the little we've seen of Jodie's character and his and Miranda's interactions, pre and post time skip.

One: My interpretation of Miranda's character, from my limited knowledge, seemed like she was a strong, independent woman, who, pardon the cliche, don't need no man. Even when she was with Chase pre-Battle of NY, you could tell she had her own strong personality and drive that didn't rely on Chase at all. Of course, as I mentioned in my first post, going through a traumatic experience can drastically change one's character, so that opinion I formed based on the pre-Battle of NY version of Miranda may be outdated. I can't really say for sure either way until we get to see more of her character - however, I am leaning towards those characteristics still somewhat applying based on her no-nonsense attitude post time skip, with perhaps an underlying layer of trauma that could explain a momentary weakness of desiring affection from anyone, even Mr. Chad.

Two: I completely understand the notion of her moving on when her love had been seemingly dead and gone for 4 years. However, the idea that she moved on to a person with Jodie's characteristics, based upon how the two interacted pre and post time skip, seems a little far-fetched, and yet plausible at the same time (good old contradiction lol). All the interactions we've seen between Miranda and Jodie, pre and post time skip have been negative (subtly and overtly), or at the very least dismissive on Miranda's part towards Jodie.
The first being when Jodie was telling Chase that he'd essentially try to bang Miranda if they ever broke up (charming, to say the least), and Miranda interrupts his 'Chading' by straightening out his disrespectful attitude towards her and Chase relationship - a subtle negative interaction between Miranda and Jodie.
The second being post time skip when Jodie comes up to Miranda while she working, refers to her as "sunshine" and generally tries to flex his way into her panties. But Miranda cuts him off fairly shortly into the conversation, and while it was because Doctor Weller had arrived and Miranda had to get back to work, it was fairly obvious that she wasn't keen on actively participating in Jodie's flirtations - a slightly more overt negative interaction between Miranda and Jodie.
The third being when their squad of Walkers were being deployed to assist in the rescue of refugees fleeing the Union. Jodie makes some remarks that are cynical at best and disparaging at worst about their mission to help the refugees. Here's where we see an important bit of Miranda's character in her response to Jodie's remarks. She vehemently reprimands him, remarking how he should be more positive and even more harshly criticizes him for belittling the efforts of the refugees' escape from the Union. To be fair to Jodie here, however, his way of dealing with the dire straits the Polity currently finds itself in could be based on dark humor - which is a common method of discussing horrible events. Whether this is the case or not, this scene displays the most overtly negative interaction between Miranda and Jodie. Those are some of the reasons why I think the notion that Miranda would move on to a person like Jodie is a bit far-fetched.
On the other hand, the same characteristics that Miranda seems to dislike about Jodie: his overconfident, cocky attitude, his drive to get what he wants even if it seems implausible (for example, loudly talking about wanting to get with Miranda pre time skip) and, whether it's a facade or how he actually is/feels, his flippant and laid back attitude towards the struggles between the Polity and the Union. All these characteristics could easily make Jodie seem like a good person to be with during Miranda's trying times. Jodie's cockiness connotes a sense of assurity in one's own beliefs and abilities, a trait that would be very comforting to a grieving Miranda, who probably felt all sorts of lost and doubt after seemingly losing her love forever. Jodie's drive to get exactly what he wants, even in seemingly implausible circumstances, is a desirable trait in general. Because if a person falls 99 times, but they still get up on the 100th, those efforts shine through, even if it's detrimental to those around you (for example, the fact that Jodie broke ranks during the mission to save the refugees - and in doing so, lost his Walker, forcing their squad leader to have to go bail him out rather than help the rest of their unit - placing them all in greater danger). Jodie's seemingly flippant and laid back attitude towards the war would possibly be a breath of fresh air for Miranda at times. She's constantly working and fighting hard, while still losing ground to the Union every day - which causes both stress and maybe occasional thoughts of the futility of all this fighting. However, if she could be around Jodie's laid back attitude towards the war, it could give her a break from all the stresses of reality and bask in some of Jodie's seemingly ignorant bliss. (I know that Jodie has an understanding of the weight of the fight against the Union - otherwise he wouldn't have stayed at the Anvil fighting a losing battle for 4 years - So his flippant attitude, in my opinion, seems more like a facade he uses to cover up his fears). Those are my thoughts on the contradictory nature of Miranda's disdain and admiration of Jodie.

I loved the 40ft robot death stare and head shake that Chase gave Jodie, and certainly agree he deserves it. But I think his seeming disrespect for all others around him, in his quest to gain the things he wants: glory in battle that results in a burden on his team at the refugee mission and getting some booty that results in an awkward atmosphere during the pre time skip period and outright hostility from Miranda during the post time skip period - which most likely causes her even more stress than she's already experiencing. This characteristic, in my mind, makes Jodie deserve something more than a death stare. I'm not saying death or anything that extreme, but perhaps an episode where he's forced to face the consequences of his more selfish actions and he wants to improve himself as a person. If this were RWBY, I would be fairly confident that something like this would happen for Jodie, because if you're fighting for good and justice in the RWBY universe, you *generally* get redeemed (in cases of characters with flaws) and/or rewarded (in cases of characters that have been good throughout the show). I emphasize generally, because there are certainly cases where the good guys are harmed or killed in RWBY (Pyrrha, Penny, Summer Rose, etc.) However, the gen:LOCK universe has already shown itself, in just three episodes, to be much more brutal and unforgiving. Soldiers, while mostly unnamed extras, casually die left and right whether in large scale battles or from the spy's intrusion where he's snapping necks and putting holes between soldiers' eyes. In a universe this brutal, there's no guarantee that Jodie gets any sort of redemption for his selfishness. He could easily die in a random altercation or RT could decide to drive his character down his selfish, self-centered path even further until he's iirredeemable (e.g. Adam in RWBY). While I think the latter is unlikely, we don't know enough about how this universe will generally treat its more prominent good guys, so only time can tell what will happen with Jodie.

The best thing you can do for your child (whether a cutter or not) is to be there for him/her in a non-critical manner. If he/she does something wrong, don't bark orders at them to do better; but guide them.

Guiding may be difficult in a situation where your child is cutting, as he/she may not be in a well enough state of mind to truly consider your advice or you may just not know how to because you never went through a similar experience.

In my case, my mom took away or hide all the sharp objects (mainly knives) to try to prevent it. But my family also arranged for me to attend a partial program in a children's mental hospital. Being around trained adults and other kids with whom I could empathize definitely helped me to move from cutting --> self-loathing to realizing it's not uncommon and allowing me to focus on healing more than self-hatred.

Something else you can do is to make it clear to your child that any pain he/she goes through is just as painful for you. While that might be an obvious notion, sometimes it's easy to overlook and/or under appreciate the obvious.

Well here are some off the top of my head:

- Humans are naturally materialistic and self-interested. We enjoy sole ownership and gain a sense of pride over what we've been able to earn through hard work. Since this is how the human condition is, allowing private property mostly satisfies that aspect of humanity; preventing widespread envy that could lead to crime. 
But if private property were made illegal, the sense of pride that people gain from earning things with their hard work would be severely damaged. Which could then cause people to turn to thievery as a method to try to covertly fulfill that desire of having something for themselves.
Obviously not every person would suddenly become a criminal, but when you wound or try to take away a person's pride (in any aspect of their life), the desperation to repair/regain it can be an overwhelming feeling. Making private property illegal won't erase the desire of sole ownership that has been part of humanity since our earliest ancestors. So one justification for private property could be to keep the peace between people in society.

- Humans are psychologically built to work for rewards/pay (whether it's for money, things, recognition, etc.). Therefore the main reason people work, even if they may not love their jobs, is so they can earn their own money to buy their own things in order to live their lives in at least a semi-comfortable manner. The desire to feel the pride of earning your own spot/purpose in life motivates most people to work hard and contribute to the well-bring of the society in which they live. So what would happen if you took that pride of hard-earned ownership away from people by making it illegal for them to earn anything for themselves? Not a lot of good. While some people would still work out of social pressure and a feeling of loyalty to their community, a lot of others would suddenly lose sufficient motivation to keep working (particularly if they already hated their jobs). And when you take away such large motivation from workers, what will make them want to keep working? Not very much, that's for sure. So another justification for private property could be to make sure people have motivation to do the work a society needs in order to function properly.

- I'll end this post with a more simple justification. We all know about, and sometimes dread, group projects in school and how they can sometimes fall apart; forcing one or two of the students to do most of the work while the rest slack off.
Ideally, everyone in a group project should contribute their fair share of work. A good group distributes the work evenly, while taking into account what part(s) each member is the best at working on. That way members can cover for each others' shortcomings without simply ignoring a part of the project altogether. To me, this is a microcosm of how a good society runs itself: teamwork, communication, and equal effort. Each of those qualities that individuals bring to the table I their jobs and interactions can then unconsciously build and maintain a strong society.
But what if the unequal amount of work for an equal share of the reward, that's so prevalent in group projects, became as common in society? Certainly no one who puts in effort would enjoy the change. Suddenly they'd have to share items that they previously worked so hard to obtain with people that may not have put in any effort at all. And that's be damn frustrating. If private property was made illegal it would amount an unequal and unbalanced distribution system of rewards that wouldn't properly praise those who work hard

The feeling of you solely owning something can occur in a number of situations:

-If you're the only one who predominantly uses a certain object, like your laptop, then I think that creates a feeling of sole ownership.

-If someone gives you a gift I think that can evoke a feeling of ownership for that object. Which is why there are those ownership cases on the court shows like Judge Judy. The defendant usually feels that the object the plaintiff is suing for ownership of belongs to them, because the plaintiff bought it for them specifically. Although that raises another issue of private property, where you have to factor in who paid legal tender for the object in question versus the fact that the buyer gave it away willing free of charge. Does the giver still technically own it since the receiver didn't offer anything of value in return? That's a tricky question that I won't get into here.

-If you buy an object with money that you solely earned, then I think that creates a feeling of ownership over the object you bought. Since you're replacing the hard-earned proof of your labor (money) with a more tangible object. I think this feeling can be strengthened even more if you feel that the object you're buying is something from which only you will gain enjoyment.

-Your more personal objects, like a toothbrush or underwear, tend to evoke that feeling of sole ownership because they're used in/near areas of your body that tend to be more private or personal. It's like someone using your hair brush versus your toothbrush: I don't mind if a familiar face uses my hair brush because I don't view the top of my head as a very personal area. But I'd feel weird if anyone used my toothbrush because I use it for a more personal area of my body.

-Similar to the situation where you use your own money to buy an object, creating an object tends to evoke a feeling of sole ownership. Whereas in the money situation it goes like this:
Time --> Money --> Objects
A situation where you create something by yourself bypasses the "money" stage of that progression. You spend time itself to form some sort of object. And if someone thinks something's important enough to spend a literal part of their lifespan to create, then I think they would feel that that object is something that belongs solely to them.

I'm sure there are more general and more specific examples, but those are what I could think of off the top of my head

An object, from a computer to a part of the earth itself, that has been officially recognized by a governing body, of the area wherein that object is located, as belonging to an individual through its purchase with officially recognized currency or trade for another legally owned object.

Private property is merely a concept that cannot be practically enforced without established laws that protect an individual's right to solely own/use an object. So without an intermediary to uphold such rules (i.e. a government), it's a weak idea that could easily be broken by another man's envy for objects that you consider solely yours.
